title: Saying the opposite correctly
objectives: Negate a statement with quantifiers and implications without changing its meaning by accident.

screens.title: One trade is enough
screens.prose: A colleague claims: **every trade today was profitable**. Here are today's six trades.
screens.question: Tap one trade that shows the claim is false.

hints.text: A profitable trade made more than £0.
Look for a trade that did not make money.
T5 lost £80. T3 made £0, which is not a profit either.

feedback.correct: One unprofitable trade sinks the claim.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find a trade that did not make more than £0.

byKey.r5: T6 made £15, a profit. Small, but still a profit.
byKey.too-many: One trade is enough. A single unprofitable trade already makes the claim false.

explain.text: T5 lost money and T3 broke even, so either one refutes the claim. To deny “every trade was profitable”, one trade that was not is enough.

screens.title: The opposite
screens.prose: Another colleague says the opposite of the claim is **every trade today lost money**.
screens.question: Which sentence is true exactly when the claim is false?

options.text: Some trade today was not profitable
Every trade today lost money
options.why: You flipped every trade. Today both are false: the claim fails, and T1 made money.

options.text: Some trade today lost money
options.why: You treated “not profitable” as “lost”. If T5 had made money, T3's £0 alone would break the claim, yet no trade lost.

options.text: No trade today was profitable
options.why: That says every trade failed. One failure is enough to deny the claim.

hints.text: The claim fails as soon as one trade is not profitable.
Not profitable includes breaking even.
“Some trade was not profitable” is false only when every trade was profitable.

feedback.correct: Right. “Some trade was not profitable” is the exact opposite.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the sentence that is true whenever at least one trade is not profitable.

byKey.some-lost: You turned “not profitable” into “lost money”. T3's £0 is not profitable and not a loss.

explain.text: The negation of “every trade was profitable” is “some trade was not profitable”. Breaking even counts, so “some trade lost money” is too strong. “Every trade lost money” is far too strong.

screens.title: Rules for not
screens.prose: You just used a rule: $\lnot(\forall x\ P(x))$ is $\exists x\ \lnot P(x)$. Its partner is $\lnot(\exists x\ P(x))$, which is $\forall x\ \lnot P(x)$. Moving $\lnot$ past a quantifier flips it.
screens.question: Negate: **some trade today lost more than £500**.

options.text: No trade today lost more than £500
Some trade today lost at most £500
options.why: You negated the inside but kept “some”. Passing $\lnot$ through $\exists$ turns it into $\forall$.

options.text: Every trade today lost more than £500
options.why: You flipped “some” to “every” but did not negate the inside.

options.text: Some trade today did not lose money
options.why: You negated “lost” instead of “lost more than £500”, and kept “some”.

hints.text: The claim is $\exists x\ P(x)$. Its negation is $\forall x\ \lnot P(x)$.
Every trade must fail to lose more than £500.
“Every trade lost at most £500” is the same as “no trade lost more than £500”.

feedback.correct: Right. $\lnot \exists$ becomes $\forall \lnot$: no trade lost more than £500.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Flip the quantifier and negate the inside.

byKey.some-le: You kept the $\exists$. A single small loss does not deny that some trade lost more than £500.

explain.text: $\lnot(\exists x\ P(x))$ is $\forall x\ \lnot P(x)$: every trade lost at most £500. Today it is true, since the worst loss was £80.

screens.title: Back to the traders
screens.prose: Claim A was $\forall t\ \exists d\ P(t, d)$: **every trader made more than £100 on some day**. It is true for this table.
screens.question: Which sentence is the negation of claim A?

options.text: Some trader made at most £100 on every day
Some trader made at most £100 on some day
options.why: You flipped “every trader” but kept “some day”. The $\lnot$ must pass both quantifiers.

options.text: No trader made more than £100 on any day
options.why: You negated the inside of every trader at once. The negation needs only one trader to fail.

options.text: Every trader made at most £100 on every day
options.why: You kept “every trader”. Passing $\lnot$ through $\forall$ turns it into $\exists$.

hints.text: Move $\lnot$ past $\forall t$, then past $\exists d$, flipping each.
$\lnot \forall t\ \exists d\ P$ becomes $\exists t\ \forall d\ \lnot P$.
Some trader, on every day, made at most £100. Check the grid: is there such a row?

feedback.correct: Right. And it is false here: every row has a value above £100, as it must be.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Flip both quantifiers and negate the inside.

byKey.inner: You negated only the first quantifier. “Some day” must become “every day” too.

explain.text: The negation is $\exists t\ \forall d\ \lnot P(t, d)$: some trader never cleared £100. Every row has a value above £100, so the negation is false. Claim A is true, so its negation had to be false.

canvas.caption: Every row has a value above £100

screens.title: Negating an inequality
screens.prose: The open sentence $x < 5$ has the truth set shown: every number below 5, with 5 itself left out.
screens.question: What is the negation of $x < 5$?

options.why: You left out $x = 5$. The number 5 is not below 5, so it belongs in the negation.

options.text: $x \ge 5$
$x \le 5$
options.why: That keeps every number below 5. A negation must be true exactly where the original is false.
You negated the number, not the sentence. The negation is about the same $x$ and the same 5.

hints.text: The negation is true exactly where $x < 5$ is false.
Is $5 < 5$ true?
$5 < 5$ is false, so 5 belongs in the negation, along with everything above it.

feedback.correct: Right. Not below 5 means 5 or more.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the value $x = 5$.

byKey.gt: You dropped $x = 5$. Since $5 < 5$ is false, 5 must be in the negation.

explain.text: The negation holds wherever $x < 5$ fails: at 5 and everything above it. That is $x \ge 5$, the closed ray from 5.

canvas.caption: $x < 5$ and its negation $x \ge 5$ share no number

screens.title: Breaking a rule
screens.prose: A desk rule: **if the spread widens, we cut the position**. The risk manager asks what a breach of the rule looks like.
screens.question: Which sentence is the negation of the rule?

options.text: The spread widened and we did not cut
If the spread widens, we do not cut
options.why: You negated only the conclusion. That is a new rule, not a breach of the old one; on Thursday both rules are kept.

options.text: If the spread does not widen, we do not cut
options.why: You negated both parts. That is the inverse, which the rule never mentioned.

options.text: The spread did not widen and we cut
options.why: Cutting when nothing happened breaks no rule. Wednesday is allowed.

hints.text: On which day was the rule broken?
From If, then: $P \Rightarrow Q$ is false only when $P$ is true and $Q$ false.
Tuesday: the spread widened and the desk did not cut. That is $P \land \lnot Q$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the day that breaks the rule and describe it.

byKey.imp-not: You wrote another “if, then”. A negation describes a breach: the spread widened and we did not cut.
byKey.inverse: You negated both parts and kept the “if”. That is the inverse; the rule says nothing about calm days.

explain.text: The rule fails only on the row where the spread widened and the desk did not cut. So $\lnot(P \Rightarrow Q)$ is $P \land \lnot Q$, not another implication.

screens.title: One step at a time
screens.prose: Over the integers, negate $\forall x\ \exists y,\ y > x$. Move $\lnot$ inward one step at a time, and stop when it sits on the inequality alone.
screens.question: Reach the negation with no $\lnot$ left.

ops.label: Move $\lnot$ past $\forall x$, which becomes $\exists x$
Drop $\lnot$ and swap $\forall$ with $\exists$
ops.why: Swapping the quantifiers is not negating. $\lnot$ must pass each quantifier in turn, flipping it as it goes.

ops.label: Negate only the inequality
ops.why: That leaves both quantifiers as they were. $\lnot$ has to pass $\forall x$ and $\exists y$ first.

ops.label: Move $\lnot$ past $\exists y$, which becomes $\forall y$
Move $\lnot$ past $\exists y$, keeping $\exists y$
ops.why: Passing $\exists$ flips it: no $y$ works means every $y$ fails.

ops.label: Write $\lnot(y > x)$ as $y < x$
ops.why: That leaves out $y = x$. Not greater than means less than or equal to.

hints.text: The outermost quantifier is $\forall x$. Deal with it first.
Each time $\lnot$ passes a quantifier, $\forall$ and $\exists$ swap.
Pass $\forall x$, then $\exists y$, then rewrite $\lnot(y > x)$ as $y \le x$.

feedback.correct: $\exists x\ \forall y,\ y \le x$: some integer is at least every integer.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move $\lnot$ past one quantifier at a time.

byKey.s1: Keep going. $\lnot$ still has $\exists y$ to pass.
byKey.s2: One step left: rewrite $\lnot(y > x)$ without the $\lnot$.

explain.text: The negation says there is a largest integer. That is false, since $x + 1$ beats any $x$. So the original statement is true, as the last lesson found.

screens.title: A preview of limits
screens.prose: In Analysis, a sequence $u_n$ tends to $L$ when $\forall \varepsilon > 0\ \exists N\ \forall n > N,\ |u_n - L| < \varepsilon$. We do not define limits here. We only negate the sentence, which says what failing to tend to $L$ means.
screens.question: Build the negation from the chips. Some chips are not needed.

hints.text: Three quantifiers, so $\lnot$ flips three times. The order stays the same.
$\forall \varepsilon$ becomes $\exists \varepsilon$, $\exists N$ becomes $\forall N$, $\forall n$ becomes $\exists n$.
$\exists \varepsilon > 0\ \forall N\ \exists n > N,\ |u_n - L| \ge \varepsilon$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Flip each quantifier in order, then negate the inequality.

byKey.le_eps: You negated $\varepsilon > 0$. That condition names which $\varepsilon$ we range over; it stays as it is.
byKey.gt: You used $>$. Not less than $\varepsilon$ means at least $\varepsilon$, so $\ge$.
byKey.fa_eps: You kept $\forall \varepsilon$. The first quantifier must flip too.
byKey.ex_N: You kept $\exists N$. Passing $\lnot$ turns it into $\forall N$.

explain.text: Each quantifier flips and keeps its place and its condition: $\varepsilon > 0$ and $n > N$ stay. Then $\lnot(|u_n - L| < \varepsilon)$ becomes $|u_n - L| \ge \varepsilon$.

screens.title: The rules
screens.prose:
Each negation moved $\lnot$ inward:

$$\lnot \forall x\ P(x) \Leftrightarrow \exists x\ \lnot P(x), \qquad \lnot \exists x\ P(x) \Leftrightarrow \forall x\ \lnot P(x)$$

$$\lnot(P \land Q) \Leftrightarrow \lnot P \lor \lnot Q, \qquad \lnot(P \Rightarrow Q) \Leftrightarrow P \land \lnot Q$$
screens.question: Which are correct negations? Select all that apply.

options.text: The negation of “every bond paid its coupon” is “some bond missed its coupon”
The negation of “some order filled” is “no order filled”
The negation of “if VaR rises, we hedge” is “VaR rose and we did not hedge”
The negation of “if VaR rises, we hedge” is “if VaR rises, we do not hedge”
options.why: You negated only the conclusion. A breach is VaR rising with no hedge.

options.text: The negation of “the price rose and volume fell” is “the price fell and volume rose”
options.why: You negated each part but kept **and**. De Morgan switches it to **or**, and “did not rise” includes staying flat.

feedback.correct: Right. Three correct negations, each from one rule.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Apply one rule to each sentence.

byKey.impbad: You kept the “if”. The negation of an implication is an **and**: $P \land \lnot Q$.

explain.text: $\lnot \forall$ becomes $\exists \lnot$, and $\lnot \exists$ becomes $\forall \lnot$. An implication's negation is $P \land \lnot Q$. An **and** negates to an **or** of the negated parts.

screens.title: The auditor's job
screens.prose: A desk head claims: **every desk stayed within its limit on every day this month**. An auditor wants to show the claim is false. Here is one week of the records.
screens.question: What must the auditor produce to show the claim is false?

options.text: One record of one desk over its limit on one day
A breach on every day of the month
options.why: You negated “every day” into “every day”. The negation needs only some day.

options.text: A breach by every desk
options.why: You kept “every desk”. The negation needs only some desk.

options.text: Records showing most days were within limit
options.why: Those records support the claim. Denying it needs a breach, not a majority.

hints.text: The claim is $\forall$ desk $\forall$ day. Negate it.
$\lnot \forall k\ \forall d$ becomes $\exists k\ \exists d$ with the limit breached.
Some desk breached on some day. One such record is enough, such as Rates on Wednesday.

feedback.correct: Right. The negation is $\exists$ desk $\exists$ day with a breach, so one record does it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Negate both quantifiers and ask what one example must show.

byKey.every-day: You kept a $\forall$. One breach on one day already makes the claim false.

explain.text: The claim is $\forall k\ \forall d$, within limit. Its negation is $\exists k\ \exists d$, over the limit. The Rates desk on Wednesday is that single record.

canvas.caption: Rates, Wednesday: one breach refutes the claim

ideas: $\lnot \forall x\ P(x)$ is $\exists x\ \lnot P(x)$, and $\lnot \exists x\ P(x)$ is $\forall x\ \lnot P(x)$. Each quantifier flips and keeps its place.
$\lnot(P \Rightarrow Q)$ is $P \land \lnot Q$: a breach, not another rule. $\lnot(P \land Q)$ is $\lnot P \lor \lnot Q$.
“Not profitable” is not “a loss”, and not $x < 5$ is $x \ge 5$. Negate exactly, boundary included.

formula.name: Negating quantifiers
formula.tex: \lnot\, \forall x\ \exists y\ P(x, y) \Leftrightarrow \exists x\ \forall y\ \lnot P(x, y)

summary.trap: The negation of “if $P$ then $Q$” is “$P$ and not $Q$”, never another “if”.

quiz.prose: Claim: **there is a stock in the fund that rose on every day this week**.
quiz.question: Which sentence is its negation?

options.text: Every stock in the fund failed to rise on some day this week
There is a stock that failed to rise on some day
options.why: You kept “there is a stock”. $\lnot \exists$ becomes $\forall \lnot$.

options.text: Every stock in the fund fell on every day
options.why: You flipped both quantifiers the wrong way. A stock needs only one day without a rise, and flat is not a fall.

options.text: No stock rose on any day this week
options.why: That is much stronger. It denies every single rise, not just a full week of rises.

feedback.correct: Right. $\lnot \exists s\ \forall d$ is $\forall s\ \exists d\ \lnot$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Flip each quantifier and negate the inside.

explain.text: The claim is $\exists s\ \forall d$, rose. Its negation is $\forall s\ \exists d$, did not rise. Each stock has at least one day without a rise.

quiz.prose: Rule: **if VaR exceeds £1m, the desk cuts risk**.
quiz.question: Which describes a breach of the rule?

options.text: VaR exceeded £1m and the desk did not cut risk
If VaR exceeds £1m, the desk does not cut risk
options.why: You wrote a new rule. A breach is one event: VaR over £1m and no cut.

options.text: VaR stayed under £1m and the desk cut risk
options.why: Cutting risk on a calm day breaks nothing.

options.text: If VaR does not exceed £1m, the desk does not cut risk
options.why: That is the inverse, not a breach.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the one case the rule forbids.

explain.text: The rule is false only when VaR exceeds £1m and the desk does not cut. That case is the negation.

options.text: $x > 2$ or $y \le 0$
$x > 2$ and $y \le 0$
options.why: You negated both parts but kept **and**. De Morgan switches it to **or**.

options.text: $x \ge 2$ or $y < 0$
options.why: You shifted the boundaries. Not $x \le 2$ is $x > 2$; not $y > 0$ is $y \le 0$.
You negated only one part.

feedback.correct: Right. Negate each part and switch **and** to **or**.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use De Morgan, then negate each inequality.

explain.text: $\lnot(A \land B)$ is $\lnot A \lor \lnot B$. Here $\lnot(x \le 2)$ is $x > 2$ and $\lnot(y > 0)$ is $y \le 0$.

options.text: $\forall x\ \exists y\ \lnot P(x, y)$
$\exists x\ \forall y\ \lnot P(x, y)$
options.why: You negated the inside but kept both quantifiers.

options.text: $\forall y\ \exists x\ \lnot P(x, y)$
options.why: You moved the variables as well. Each quantifier flips but keeps its place.

options.text: $\forall x\ \forall y\ \lnot P(x, y)$
options.why: You flipped the first quantifier only. The $\forall y$ must become $\exists y$.

feedback.correct: Right. Each quantifier flips in place, then $P$ is negated.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move $\lnot$ past each quantifier in turn.

explain.text: $\lnot \exists x$ becomes $\forall x\ \lnot$, then $\lnot \forall y$ becomes $\exists y\ \lnot$. The order of $x$ and $y$ does not change.
